title: Robotic demining: what to remove, and in what order
summary: A demining robot has to reach a PFM-1 landmine lying among leaves, branches and debris. I'm developing a hierarchical reinforcement-learning policy that decides what to remove and how, and the modular software that runs it on a UR5e arm with a Robotiq gripper — in simulation first, then on the real robot.

tldr: Humanitarian demining: the robot must free a PFM-1 landmine from clutter so it can be extracted safely.

A hierarchical policy looks at the scene and decides what to remove and how: a PPO-trained decider, a skill manager that picks a skill or a combination of skills, and learned skills such as push — all trained teacher–student.
I wrote the robot software as independent modules with explicit interfaces, so the simulator can be swapped for the real UR5e without rewriting the rest.

sections.title: The problem
body: The target is a small, scatterable plastic anti-personnel mine. Objects around it can rest on it, shield it or block the gripper, and moving the wrong one can push or drop something onto it.

The robot has to understand the scene, identify what prevents a safe extraction, decide how many objects to remove, which ones and how — grasp or push — and in what order, until the mine can be lifted out without being disturbed.

list: Observe → decide → execute. The robot perceives the scene, chooses one object at a time, acts, then checks what actually happened before deciding again.
Simulation first. Randomized cluttered scenes in MuJoCo, built from real-world object classes.
Teacher–student reinforcement learning. A teacher that sees the true simulator state trains a student that only gets what the sensors see.
Safety in the objective. The reward penalizes any disturbance of the mine and anything falling near it, and actions the gripper can't physically perform are rejected before execution.

body.alt: Diagram of the observe, decide, execute loop with the task module computing the reward
body.caption: The decision loop: each block has a defined interface, so perception, policy and robot can be developed and replaced independently.

sections.title: How the software is built
body: The robot software is a modular Python codebase: each module has one responsibility and talks to the others only through small typed contracts.

list: SCENE generates the randomized clutter; SIMULATION owns the physics. It is the only module that imports MuJoCo — everything else sees interfaces, so the simulator can be replaced by the real robot.

OBSERVE turns sensors into an Observation; DECIDE reads it and returns an ObjectDecision; EXECUTE turns that into arm and gripper motion and reports an ExecutionOutcome; TASK computes reward, success and safety metrics.
An environment wrapper exposes the loop with the Gymnasium API for training; experiments and evaluation compare policies and baselines on the same benchmark scenes.
The development phase lives in configuration, not in the code: moving from ideal to realistic perception or execution means swapping an implementation, not adding if-branches.

sections.title: Safety before every action
body: Before the arm moves, the chosen object is checked against what the sensors can see: can the gripper actually reach it, from at least one side, without hitting anything else? If not, the action is refused — the arm doesn't move, the refusal costs a small penalty and is remembered, and the policy decides again.

body.alt: Flow: observe, decide, safety check; if reachable the arm acts, otherwise the action is refused and the policy decides again
body.caption: An impossible action is rejected before anything touches the scene.

sections.title: How the policy is trained
body: The policy is hierarchical. A decider, trained with PPO, chooses which object to remove next; a skill manager chooses how — which skill, or which combination of skills — and the skills, such as push, carry it out. In simulation a teacher can see everything — exact poses, contacts, which object supports which — and only if it beats rule-based baselines on held-out scenes does it supervise the student. The student sees only sensor observations: it imitates the teacher, then keeps improving with reinforcement learning. The student is the policy meant for the real robot.

body.alt: Two rows: teacher trained on privileged state with PPO and a quality gate; student trained by imitation and PPO fine-tuning on sensor observations
body.caption: Teacher–student training: privileged information is used only to teach, never at deployment.

sections.title: Toward the real robot
body: Training runs in mjlab (MuJoCo). The same modules are then validated with ROS in Gazebo, and finally deployed on the physical UR5e with a Robotiq 2F-140 gripper.
